lesson.grammar_point: present perfect simple vs past simple

listenings.text: People always ask me how I ended up in disputes, as if there had been a plan. There was no plan. I studied tax law, I hated it, and I spent two years doing corporate deals in a firm where I was the most junior person in the room. Then a partner asked me to sit in on an arbitration because somebody was ill, and I have not really left that room since. What I would say to anybody who is early in their career is that the interesting work usually arrives by accident, and it arrives disguised as a favour you are asked to do at short notice. I have been in this practice for eighteen years now. I have taken on maybe forty cases as lead counsel, and the ones I remember are not the ones we won. They are the two or three where I understood, halfway through, that I had been arguing the wrong point for months.

Somebody asked me last week what a corporate lawyer actually does all day, and I gave the honest answer, which is that most of it is reading. I read contracts that other people wrote, I read the two paragraphs that will decide everything, and then I write a note explaining, in ordinary language, what the client has just agreed to. The calls come later. When people picture this job they picture a courtroom, and I have been in a courtroom maybe eight times in twenty years. What is demanding about it is not the drama. It is the volume, and the fact that you are juggling four matters that all became urgent on the same Tuesday afternoon. I gave up trying to protect my evenings a long time ago. What I did protect, in the end, was the first hour of the morning, and that turned out to be the thing that kept me in the profession.
